opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the most anxious periods of my early research life. When you submit your first paper, you've poured months into it. You've rerun experiments, rewritten sections, stayed up debugging at two in the morning. Then you hit submit and it's completely out of your hands. For weeks you just wait.

What made it hard was that I had no reference point. I didn't know whether the work was good enough, whether the reviewers would understand what I was trying to do, or whether I'd framed the problem the right way. As a young student, your sense of self-worth gets tied up with that one decision. If it's rejected, you start wondering whether you're cut out for research at all.

Looking back, a few things helped me get through it. First, my advisor and senior labmates kept reminding me that rejection is normal. Almost every good paper gets rejected at least once, and the review process has a lot of randomness. Hearing that from people I respected took some of the weight off.

Second, I learned to keep working instead of just refreshing my email. I started the next project and kept thinking about the problem itself. That shifted my focus from "will this get in?" to "is this direction meaningful?" The second question is much more within your control.

When the acceptance finally came, of course I was thrilled. But the bigger lesson was about the uncertainty itself. Research is fundamentally about doing things where you don't know the outcome. If you need certainty to feel okay, it's going to be a very painful career. So that first paper was also my first real training in living with uncertainty, and in trusting that if you keep working on important problems carefully, things tend to work out over the long run, even if any single result is unpredictable.

r001.rationale: The response describes anxiety and uncertainty followed by eventual acceptance, but it does not say He Wang believed the paper would never be accepted or that it was nominated for Best Paper.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the uncertainty was the hardest part, harder than the research itself. When you're writing the paper, you at least feel like you have some control. You can run another experiment, you can rewrite a paragraph, you can tighten an argument. But once you hit submit, all of that is gone. It's in someone else's hands, and you're just waiting.

I remember I checked my email constantly. I knew the decision date, and for a week before it I was basically useless. I'd open the review portal even though I knew nothing had changed. My advisor kept telling me, "Go work on the next thing," which was good advice, but I couldn't really follow it.

When the reviews came back, they were mixed. One reviewer liked it, one was lukewarm, and one had basically missed the main point of the paper. My first reaction was anger, frankly. I thought, "You didn't even read it carefully." But after a day or two I realized that if a reasonable reviewer could misunderstand it, that was partly on me. The writing wasn't clear enough. So the rebuttal became an exercise in explaining what I actually meant, and I think the paper got genuinely better because of that.

It did get accepted in the end, but what stuck with me was less the acceptance and more the realization that this uncertainty never fully goes away. Every paper after that, I still felt it. What changed was my relationship to it. I stopped treating a rejection as a judgment of whether I belonged in the field and started treating it as noise in a pretty noisy process. That shift took years, though. For the first paper, I had none of that perspective. It felt like everything was riding on it.

astra-6.text: For me, the hardest part was not having a baseline. With your first paper, you don’t really know whether the work is ready or how reviewers will respond. You can put a lot of effort into it and still feel uncertain. Getting it accepted was a relief, but until then, I had to focus on what I could control—making the argument clearer and doing the work as carefully as I could.
